lead: A physical defect can be a short, an open or a missing implant, in endless shapes and sizes, so no test program can target defects one by one. A fault model replaces them with a short logical list: a line stuck at 0 or 1, two lines bridged, a transistor that never conducts, a path that is too slow. The single stuck-at model is the workhorse of digital test; delay faults catch chips that compute the right value too late. Fault simulation and ATPG in 6.3 work on this list.
prereq: You need: logic gates and truth tables, and gate-level modelling from the Verilog chapters.

sections.h3: From physical defect to logical fault

blocks.text: A defect is physical: a metal short, an open contact, a missing implant, a pinhole in thin oxide. A fault is the logical model of that defect, for example 'line A is stuck at 0'. An error is a wrong value on some line inside the circuit, and a failure is lost function: a wrong value reaches an output pin and the chip misses its specification. A short from one input of a NAND gate to ground behaves like that input stuck at 0.

A defect has a size, a resistance and a place, and its effect changes with all three. A fault model fixes the effect, not the cause. Because the list is finite, a program can enumerate it, generate vectors for it and report fault coverage.

A line is a primary input, a primary output, a gate input or a gate output; each branch of a fanout is a separate line. A line stuck-at-0 (SA0, written A/0) always reads 0; stuck-at-1 (SA1, A/1) always reads 1. Single stuck-at means only one line is faulty at a time.

blocks.where: where N is the number of single stuck-at faults and L the number of lines; the 2 counts SA0 and SA1.

blocks.text: Two faults are equivalent if no input vector can tell their faulty circuits apart. On a two-input NAND, A/0, B/0 and Z/1 all force the output to 1 for every input, so they form one class. A/1 and B/1 are not equivalent: A/1 shows only when B = 1, and B/1 only when A = 1. Equivalence collapsing keeps one fault per class; a k-input NAND, NOR, AND or OR gate goes from 2(k + 1) faults to k + 2.

Fault f dominates fault g if every test for g also detects f. Then f can be dropped too, because the test for g catches it. On the NAND, the only test for A/1 is 01, and 01 also detects Z/0, so Z/0 dominates A/1 and is dropped.

For a whole circuit the checkpoint theorem says a test set that detects every stuck-at fault on the primary inputs and on the fanout branches detects every single stuck-at fault in the circuit. So the fault list can start from the checkpoints only. A fault that no vector can detect is called redundant; only ATPG can prove it, and coverage reports count it separately (6.3).

A transistor stuck-open never conducts; a transistor stuck-short always conducts. In static CMOS a stuck-open pMOS cuts the output off from VDD, and a stuck-open nMOS cuts it off from ground, for some input combinations. The output then floats and keeps its old value on its capacitance, so the gate behaves like a memory. A test needs two vectors: the first sets the output to a known value (say 0), the second asks the broken transistor to drive it to 1. If the output stays 0, the fault is caught. A stuck-short makes pull-up and pull-down fight; it is best caught by the large quiescent supply current it causes (IDDQ test).

A bridging fault shorts two lines. When one driver pulls 0 and the other pulls 1, the result depends on drive strength; simple models are wired-AND (0 wins) and wired-OR (1 wins). A resistive bridge may give the right logic value but slowly.

A transition delay fault makes one line slow-to-rise or slow-to-fall. A path delay fault makes a whole input-to-output path too slow, even when each gate on it is only a little slow. Both need a two-vector test applied at the rated clock: the first vector V1 sets the line to its starting value, the launch edge applies V2 and creates the transition, and the capture edge one clock period later stores the result. A slow path still holds the old value at capture.

examples.question: A two-input NAND gate has inputs A, B and output Z. (a) List every single stuck-at fault. (b) Collapse the faults by equivalence, then by dominance. (c) Give the smallest test set that detects all six faults. Write each vector as AB.
steps: Lines: A, B and Z, so N = 2 × 3 = 6 faults: A/0, A/1, B/0, B/1, Z/0, Z/1.
A/0 makes Z = 1 for every input; it differs from the good gate only at 11. B/0 and Z/1 give the same faulty table. Class {A/0, B/0, Z/1}, detected only by 11.
A/1 gives Z = NOT B: it differs only at 01 (good 1, faulty 0). B/1 differs only at 10. Z/0 differs at 00, 01 and 10. So there are 4 equivalence classes: {A/0, B/0, Z/1}, {A/1}, {B/1}, {Z/0}.
Dominance: the test for A/1 (01) also detects Z/0, so Z/0 dominates A/1 and is dropped. The collapsed list is A/0, A/1, B/1: 3 faults, which is k + 1 for k = 2 after dominance.
Each of the 3 faults has exactly one test (11, 01 and 10), so no smaller set exists. Check that {01, 10, 11} also catches Z/0: at 01 the good Z is 1 and the faulty Z is 0, so yes.
examples.answer: Six faults collapse to four equivalence classes and to three faults after dominance; the smallest complete test set is {01, 10, 11}, three vectors, and 00 is not needed.

examples.question: Line A of a two-input AND gate Z = A·B is slow-to-rise. The path from A to the capturing flip-flop normally takes 1.2 ns, and the defect adds 1.0 ns. The clock period is 2.0 ns. Give the two-vector test, and say what the flip-flop captures at speed and on a slow tester with a 10 ns period.
steps: To see a rising A, V1 must hold A = 0 and V2 must have A = 1. B must be 1 in V2 so that Z follows A. So V1 = (A, B) = (0, 1) and V2 = (1, 1).
Good circuit: Z goes 0 → 1 and settles 1.2 ns after the launch edge, before the capture edge at 2.0 ns. Captured Z = 1.
Faulty circuit: Z settles after 1.2 + 1.0 = 2.2 ns, which is 0.2 ns after the capture edge. Captured Z = 0, the old value, so the fault is detected.
Slow tester: capture comes 10 ns after launch; even the faulty Z has settled by 2.2 ns, so it captures 1 and the chip wrongly passes.
examples.answer: The test is V1 = 01, V2 = 11 at the rated 2.0 ns clock; the faulty chip captures 0 instead of 1. At a 10 ns period the same vectors miss the fault, which is why delay tests run at speed.

traps: On a two-input NAND, Z/1 is equivalent to A/0 and B/0; it is not a class of its own.
A/1 and B/1 are not equivalent on a NAND: each shows only when the other input is 1.
Counting lines without the fanout branches. Each branch is a line with its own two faults.
A stuck-open can pass a single vector, because the floating output keeps a value that may happen to be right. It needs a two-vector sequence.
Applying a delay test slowly. Launch and capture must be one rated clock period apart, or a slow path looks good.

quiz.q: Define stuck-at-0 and stuck-at-1 for a line, and say what 'single' means.
quiz.a: SA0: the line always reads 0. SA1: the line always reads 1. Single: only one line in the circuit is faulty at a time.

quiz.q: When are two stuck-at faults equivalent, and when does one dominate another?
quiz.a: Equivalent: every input vector gives the same output for both faulty circuits, so no test can tell them apart. Fault f dominates g when every test for g also detects f, so f can be dropped once g is targeted.

quiz.q: A three-input NAND gate has inputs A, B, C and output Z. How many single stuck-at faults exist, and how many remain after equivalence collapsing?
quiz.a: Lines A, B, C and Z: 2 × 4 = 8 faults. Equivalence merges A/0, B/0, C/0 and Z/1 into one class, leaving k + 2 = 5 faults.

quiz.q: In the NAND example, which vector detects A/1 and what output difference appears?
quiz.a: AB = 01. The good gate gives Z = 1; with A stuck at 1 the gate sees 11 and gives Z = 0.

quiz.q: State the difference between a transition delay fault and a path delay fault.
quiz.a: A transition delay fault makes one line slow to rise or slow to fall. A path delay fault makes one complete path from input to output too slow, even when each gate on it is only slightly slow.

quiz.q: Why may a stuck-open transistor in a CMOS gate need two vectors?
quiz.a: For some inputs the broken transistor leaves the output connected to neither rail, so the output keeps its previous value. The first vector sets that value (say 0); the second asks the broken transistor to drive the opposite value. Only the pair shows the output stuck at its old value.

quiz.q: In the second worked example the defect adds 1.0 ns. What is the smallest extra delay the 2.0 ns test can catch, and why?
quiz.a: The good path has 2.0 − 1.2 = 0.8 ns of slack. An extra delay of more than 0.8 ns moves Z past the capture edge, so about 0.8 ns is the smallest defect this test catches. Smaller defects need a longer path through the same line or a faster capture.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry now uses cell-aware fault models that list the opens and shorts inside each library cell, and FinFET defects make some faults behave differently from planar CMOS. Delay test is run at speed on most chips, and choosing which paths to test is still a research problem. Search 'cell-aware ATPG', 'transition delay test' and 'small delay defects'.
